transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-06-24
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~35 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Sam Reynolds (Acme ML Eng), Lydia Park (Acme Platform Eng), Marcus Li (Acme PM)

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
- Reviewed recent cache metrics (prefix + KV) and how prompt reuse patterns affect hit rates.
- Discussed short term tuning (TTLs, eviction) and medium term prompt canonicalization.
- Agreed on experiments and next steps (load test, pricing for dedicated cache).

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Alright hi everyone thanks for joining, uh this is the weekly caching sync for the POC. Quick roll call, Priya and I are here from Redwood. Sam, Lydia, Marcus you on?
[00:08] Sam (Acme): Yep, hey, Sam here. Lydia is on, Marcus too.
[00:12] Lydia: Hey all.
[00:14] Jordan: Awesome. Priya do you want to kick off with the metric run-down?
[00:18] Priya (Redwood): Yeah sure, um so we pulled the last 7 days of telemetry. Overall KV-plus-prefix cache combined hit rate is around 62% — so that means about 62% of tokens served had either prefix K-V cache or prefix reuse. The breakdown, and caveat this is from our instrumentation which sometimes labels routes slightly weird, is prefix-only hits ~48% and KV-only hits ~14%. There's a bit of overlap where both apply.
[00:42] Sam: 62% OK that's better than last week right? We were at like 55?
[00:46] Priya: Yeah last week was 55, so +7 points after the template dedupe change you rolled out, Sam. Good improvement.
[00:53] Marcus: Quick question, can you clarify prefix vs KV? I always mix those in the notes.
[00:58] Priya: Sure. Prefix caching is when the beginning of the prompt (system + previous messages that we canonicalize) matches an entry in the cache and we can reuse KV caches for that model's attention state. KV cache is the key-value cache for autoregressive decoding; sometimes we persist a KV snapshot for long-running sessions. The tooling sometimes transcribes K-V cash which is, uh, confusing in the UI.
[01:22] Lydia: Ha, yeah saw that typo.
[01:24] Jordan: Cool. Any major outliers in hit rate by endpoint? Priya?
[01:28] Priya: Yup. The chat assistant endpoints (customer_support and billing_bot) are the highest, ~72% combined. The personalized summary endpoint is lower, around 42%. We suspect variability in user prompt prefixes and free-form text reduces canonicalization.
[01:44] Sam: That makes sense. Our summary flow includes user-specific chunks that aren't repeated. Is there a quick way to increase the reuse without changing UX?
[01:52] Priya: A few tricks: 1) canonicalize system and instruction blocks server-side so they map to a consistent signature; 2) normalize timestamps and user IDs out of the prefix; 3) use short template tokens for common user actions rather than full sentences. Those don't need UX changes, basically preprocessing.
[02:10] Sam: Ok preprocessing seems doable. We'll need to vet with product.
[02:14] Marcus: Also curious about TTLs. What's the current TTL for prefix entries?
[02:18] Priya: Default TTL is 30 minutes for session-level prefixes, KV snapshots are 90 minutes for the POC. We tuned to a shorter TTL on high-churn routes last week which improved freshness but cost hits. If we increase TTL we'll likely see better hit rates but risk stale context for some flows.
[02:36] Lydia: Our sessions are usually short, 5-15 minutes, so 30 minutes might be overkill but not harmful.
[02:42] Jordan: Do we have any P50/P95 latency delta between cache hits and misses available?
[02:47] Priya: Yes — approximate numbers: cache-hit p50 is ~90ms, p95 ~220ms. Miss p50 is ~260ms, p95 ~700ms in the hosted POC cluster. Those are token emission latencies, so end-to-end varies with prompt length. There's obviously variance across models and sequence lengths.
[03:08] Sam: So cache is a pretty strong latency win.
[03:10] Priya: Yeah. Also note that lookups add a small overhead but it's far outweighed by skipping recomputation.
[03:16] Jordan: Any concern about cache correctness, e.g., leaking user data across sessions?
[03:20] Priya: We enforce namespace isolation per tenant and per-route keys. For the POC it's enabled. The only possible leak is if you canonicalize too aggressively and accidentally generalize sensitive tokens; that's why we recommended masking IDs and not canonicalizing user content.
[03:36] Sam: Good call. We'll be careful about masking.
[03:38] Marcus: Do you have a sense of how much extra hit-rate we could unlock with prompt canonicalization? I.e., optimistic numbers?
[03:44] Priya: From prior customers and internal tests, canonicalization plus template tokenization can add ~10-20 percentage points depending on how much repetition there is. For Acme's traffic shape I'd guess +12 points conservative, so from 62% to ~74% if you canonicalize the system/instruction blocks and normalize variable fields.
[04:02] Lydia: That's compelling.
[04:04] Jordan: Ok so immediate experiment: Sam runs a 24h test with canonicalized prompts. Priya tweaks TTLs in staging to see delta. Jordan will follow up on dedicated caching pricing. Anything else?
[04:15] Sam: One more thing — can Redwood provide per-model cache hit breakdown? We have a smaller LLM for quick responses and a larger model for long responses. We want to see which model benefits most.
[04:25] Priya: Yes we can surface per-model per-route hit rates. Right now the dashboard has combined, we'll push a per-model view and a CSV export.
[04:32] Jordan: Excellent. Also on dedicated caching, the idea is we can place a larger memory KV store co-located with the serving pods; that helps with higher TTLs and fewer evictions, but there's a cost tradeoff which I'll detail in the pricing note.
[04:46] Marcus: Would the dedicated option be required to get >80% hit rate? Or can hosted reach that?
[04:52] Priya: Hosted can reach high hit rates with canonicalization and TTL tuning, but dedicated reduces evictions under heavy tail and lets you increase retention (bigger working set). If you have lots of long-running sessions, dedicated helps.
[05:04] Sam: For our use case we have a mix. We should test both.
[05:08] Jordan: Agreed. We'll scope a benchmark that compares hosted tuned vs dedicated baseline.
[05:12] Priya: On instrumentation notes — watch for false positives in our current logs where system prompts include timestamps. That kills the prefix match and inflates miss rate. We can add a normalization pass to strip common ephemeral values.
[05:26] Lydia: We'll send examples of offending prompts.
[05:29] Marcus: Any blockers on the security or compliance side for retaining KV snapshots?
[05:33] Priya: For the POC we've got tenant encryption at rest, RBAC for access, and audit logs. For production you'd want KMS-backed keys and maybe HSM if required. We can send the SOC2/ISO notes. Jordan will attach the security docs.
[05:47] Jordan: Yep I'll follow up with the security pack.
[05:50] Sam: One tiny thing — sometimes the transcripts say K-V cash which is funny; don't let the UI show that.
[05:56] Priya: Noted, we'll fix the label.
[05:58] Jordan: Cool. Let's go into a quick walkthrough of the recent experiment results — Priya?
[06:03] Priya: We rolled two changes last week: 1) dedupe identical system prompts across sessions, 2) turned on normalization for dates in the instruction block. The direct effect: +7 points overall. The dashboard is linked in the doc — Redwood dashboard //grafana/redwood/acme-poc (note: live link). The CSV export shows per-route breakdown; the chat routes improved the most. There's some noise in the summary endpoint due to user-inserted long text chunks.
[06:33] Sam: Does the CSV show sample prompts that matched? That would help us prioritize template changes.
[06:37] Priya: Yes, we included sample signatures. But there is PII redaction in the export.
[06:42] Marcus: On the canonicalization path, what's the recommended tooling? Is this something Redwood provides or do we need to implement?
[06:49] Priya: We provide a canonicalization library as part of the SDK; it can run as middleware to normalize prompts (remove timestamps, replace user ids with tokens). For quick POC you can use the SDK. For full control you can implement server-side preprocessing.
[07:02] Sam: We'll try the SDK first.
[07:05] Jordan: Ok any concerns about function-calling and canonicalization? We rely on structured tool outputs in a few flows.
[07:12] Priya: For function/tool calling you want to treat the tool schema as part of the signature. We don't canonicalize arguments by default. The safe path is to canonicalize the wrapper text and keep tool payloads intact.
[07:24] Lydia: Good to know.
[07:26] Marcus: What's the approximate cost delta if we bump TTLs from 30->90 minutes?
[07:31] Priya: Rough estimate for your traffic shape: compute cost drops by ~8-12% due to higher hit rates but storage/working set memory cost rises; net could be neutral or slightly positive depending on eviction pressure. Jordan will provide a more precise estimate in the pricing note.
[07:48] Jordan: We'll model a 30/60/90 minute scenario in the note.
[07:53] Sam: Great. A few housekeeping Qs: can you give us the raw histograms for latency and the export format we can hook into our perf tracker?
[07:59] Priya: Yes, we'll push p50/p95 histograms, token-level latencies and the CSV.
[08:05] Jordan: Alright last bit — timeline and owners. Review the action items: Priya change TTLs and push dashboard, Jordan pricing + security docs, Sam run canonicalized load test, Lydia provide top endpoints. Any changes?
[08:17] Sam: Sounds right.
[08:18] Lydia: Yep.
[08:19] Marcus: Yep.
[08:20] Jordan: Perfect. We'll reconvene same time next week. Thanks everyone.
[08:24] Priya: Thanks all.
[34:45] (recording continued silent notes and end)
